facts.statement: Wellnhopterus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian),

facts.statement: This azhdarchid pterosaur lived in what is now Texas, United States.
facts.quote: Wellnhopterus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Texas, United States.

facts.statement: Fossils of Wellnhopterus were discovered in the Javelina Formation at Big Bend National Park in Brewster County, Texas.
facts.quote: Its fossil remains were discovered in the Javelina Formation at Big Bend National Park, located in Brewster County, Texas.

facts.statement: The species was formally named and described in December 2021 by Brian Andres and Wann Langston Jr.
facts.quote: It was not until December 2021 that they were given a new genus and type species, Wellnhopterus brevirostris, named and described by paleontologists Brian Andres and, posthumously, Wann Langston Jr..

facts.statement: The fossil remains were discovered in March 1986 by preparator Robert Rainey.
facts.quote: In March 1986, the remains of jaws and cervical (neck) vertebrae of a large pterosaur were discovered in the Javelina Formation at Big Bend National Park in Brewster County, western Texas, by preparator Robert Rainey.

facts.statement: In 1996, researchers noted the fossils came from older layers than Quetzalcoatlus and featured a shorter snout and neck.
facts.quote: In 1996, paleontologists Alexander Kellner and Wann Langston Jr. pointed out that the remains dated from older layers than those which had produced Quetzalcoatlus sp. and that it represented a pterosaur with a shorter snout and neck.

facts.statement: In 2013, Brian Andres analyzed the fossils and classified them as azhdarchids.
facts.quote: However, the fossils were studied in 2013 by American paleontologist Brian Andres, whose cladistic analysis recovered the taxon as a member of the family Azhdarchidae, both when the cervical vertebrae were included and when only the skull material was entered in the analysis.

facts.statement: The known fossils include a set of jaws, several neck vertebrae, and a fragmentary long bone.
facts.quote: The known fossil remains of Wellnhopterus consist of specimen TxVP 42489-2, which is a set of upper and lower jaws, specimens TxVP 42489-2.3 to 42489-2.8, which are several cervical vertebrae, and specimen TxVP 42489-2.9, which is a fragmentary long bone.

facts.statement: Researchers estimated its wingspan to be about 3 meters, classifying it as a mid-sized pterosaur.
facts.quote: In its description, Andres and Langston Jr. estimated a wingspan of about 3 m, making it a mid-sized pterosaur.

facts.statement: Wellnhopterus had a blunt snout and a robust, short neck, contrasting with the slender jaws and long neck of Quetzalcoatlus.
facts.quote: The blunt structure of the snout, coupled with the more robustly-built and shorter neck of Wellnhopterus is quite different from the contemporary azhdarchid Quetzalcoatlus, which had more slender jaws and a longer neck.

facts.statement: Its jaws show well-defined bluntness and it possesses a stockier, shorter neck compared to Quetzalcoatlus.
facts.quote: With regards to the structure of its snout, Wellnhopterus has a well-defined bluntness in its jaws and a stockier and shorter neck, which is very different from the slender-jawed and longer-necked structure of its coeval Quetzalcoatlus.

facts.statement: It is classified in the family Azhdarchidae, though its exact position within the group is debated.
facts.quote: Wellnhopterus has been assigned to the family Azhdarchidae, but its position within the group has been somewhat disputed.

facts.statement: The 2021 description placed Wellnhopterus within the family Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: In its description in 2021 by Andres and Langston Jr., Wellnhopterus was recovered as a member of the family Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: A 2023 study by Rubi Pêgas and colleagues recovered Wellnhopterus in a different position than the original 2021 analysis.
facts.quote: In 2023, paleontologist Rubi Pêgas and colleagues performed their own phylogenetic analysis and recovered Wellnhopterus in a much more different position than Andres in 2021.

facts.statement: Recent analyses place it in a basal position outside the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae, forming a group with Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho.
facts.quote: Within Azhdarchidae, it formed a trichotomy with both Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho. This clade, which was joined by Eurazhdarcho, was recovered outside Quetzalcoatlinae in a more basal (primitive) position.

facts.statement: It is likely that Wellnhopterus was a raptorial predator specializing in large prey.
facts.quote: Wellnhopterus was likely raptorial, as "blunt-jawed" azhdarchids are thought to have been specialized to hunt proportionally large prey.

facts.statement: A separate genus named Javelinadactylus was briefly assigned to these fossils in July 2021 before the paper was retracted.
facts.quote: Back in July 2021, the jaw remains of Wellnhopterus had actually been given a separate genus and type species, "Javelinadactylus sagebieli", named and described by paleontologist Hebert Campos. He assigned it to the group Thalassodrominae. The article describing it, however, has now been retracted due to Campos lacking ownership of the reported data and because Andres had submitted his paper describing Wellnhopterus earlier than he did.

facts.statement: An early reconstruction of Quetzalcoatlus based on these fossils depicted a snout that was too blunt, an error repeated in many popular works.
facts.quote: In the photo caption, Wellnhofer assigned it to Quetzalcoatlus sp., indicating an indeterminate species of said pterosaur. Accordingly, his illustrator John Sibbick reconstructed Quetzalcoatlus itself with a snout that was too blunt, a mistake repeated in many popular science works.

facts.statement: Its coexistence with larger pterosaurs suggests that pterosaur diversity in the Maastrichtian was higher than previously thought.
facts.quote: Its co-existence with the much larger Quetzalcoatlus and a possible additional pterosaur taxon in the Javelina Formation have been used as examples of pterosaur diversity being higher in the Maastrichtian than traditionally thought.

facts.statement: Wellnhopterus belongs to the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Quetzalcoatlinae

facts.statement: The genus is classified within the family Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: Wellnhopterus is a member of the class Reptilia.
